after: ## 7.1 Why was imperialism a significant force in Africa from 1870?
alt: Three motive cards: economic (raw materials, gold and diamonds, Hobson's surplus capital), religious and cultural (missionaries and the civilising mission) and national and strategic (prestige for Germany and Italy). Below, Britain's strategic chain: the route to India through the Suez Canal led to buying the Khedive's shares (1875), occupying Egypt (1882), and concern for the Nile and the Sudan.
caption: Three kinds of motive; for Britain, strategy led from Suez to the Sudan.

after: ## 7.1 Why was imperialism a significant force in Africa from 1870?
alt: Two chains of command. Direct rule, as in French assimilation or the Congo Free State: European officials replace local rulers. Indirect rule, associated with Lugard in Northern Nigeria: a few officials supervise existing chiefs and emirs. A note says indirect rule was cheaper but froze local hierarchies.
caption: Direct rule replaced local rulers; indirect rule worked through them.

after: ## 7.1 Why was imperialism a significant force in Africa from 1870?
alt: A table of four cases: the Zulu won at Isandlwana but lost at Ulundi (1879); the Ndebele rebellion (1896-97) was crushed; Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa (March 1896); the Herero War (1904-07) ended with most Herero dead. Below, modern rifles, unity and numbers explain Ethiopia's success.
caption: Resistance usually failed; Adwa shows what success required.

after: ## 7.2 What was the impact of imperial expansion on international relations?
alt: After a note on Egypt (1882) and the Berlin Conference (1884-85), a vertical timeline from 1896 to 1912 drawn to scale. On the left, clashes: the Kruger Telegram (1896), Weltpolitik and the Navy Laws, Fashoda (1898), the Boer War, and the Moroccan crises of 1905-06 and 1911. On the right, agreements: the Anglo-Japanese Treaty (1902), the Entente Cordiale (1904), Algeciras (1906) and the November 1911 convention.
caption: Colonial disputes were settled by agreement, but the agreements built rival blocs.

after: ## 7.3 Why did Japan emerge as a world power?
alt: A vertical timeline from 1850 to 1920 drawn to scale. On the left, reform and relations: Perry (1853-54), the unequal treaties, the Meiji Restoration (1868), conscription (1873), the constitution (1889), the Anglo-Japanese Treaty (1902) and treaty revision (1911). On the right, expansion: war with China (1894-95), victory over Russia (1904-05), Korea (1905, 1910), the First World War gains and Siberia (1918).
caption: Decades of reform came before Japan's military victories.

after: ## 7.4 Why did the USA emerge as a world power?
alt: A vertical timeline from 1890 to 1918 drawn to scale. Ideas and triggers on the left: the closed frontier (1890), Turner and the Panic of 1893, the Cuban rising (1895), the Maine (February 1898), the Lusitania (May 1915), and U-boats and the Zimmermann Telegram (February-March 1917). Actions on the right: war with Spain (1898), the Philippine-American War, the Platt Amendment, Panama, the Great White Fleet, Nicaragua (1912), the canal (1914) and war (April 1917).
caption: Two bursts of activity: 1898-1903 overseas expansion, and 1917 entry into world war.

alt: Four reasons in two linked pairs. Isolation exposed by the Boer War and naval overstretch made an alliance necessary. Russia's advance into Manchuria and Japan's rise as a credible partner made Japan the obvious ally. Both lines lead to the Anglo-Japanese Treaty of 1902.
caption: Isolation plus overstretch made an alliance necessary; Russia made Japan the ally.
